title: the Sama Veda as song
hook: the Chandogya Upanishad, a text of the Sama Veda, follows a chain from the ground under your feet to the high chant, link by link

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song: verses from the Rig Veda, set to melody, opening with come, Agni, to the feast. Did you say one ordinary sentence like it was worth singing? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

Orange juice in a carton. Before that, oranges in a crate. Before that, a tree. Before that, rain and soil. Every glass at breakfast sits at the end of a chain, and on a busy morning nobody follows it back. One old text follows a chain like that, link by link, from the ground up. But it isn't tracing breakfast. It's tracing a song. The Chandogya Upanishad belongs to the Sama Veda, the Veda of melody. And right at its start, it asks what the very best part of everything is, and keeps going until it reaches the chant itself. Today: the chain that ends in a song.
screen: `A GLASS OF JUICE, A CHAIN BEHIND IT.` → `ONE TEXT TRACES A SONG.` → `THE CHAIN THAT ENDS IN A CHANT.`

segments.voice: The Chandogya opens with the udgitha, the high chant, the part of a Sama Veda song the lead singer sends up. It says, in paraphrase: let a person meditate on the syllable Om as the udgitha, for the chant begins with Om. Then comes the chain. The essence of all beings is the earth. The essence of the earth is water. Of water, plants. Of plants, the human being. Of the human being, speech. Of speech, the Rig Veda's verses. Of the Rig Veda, the Sama Veda, the saman, the melody. And of the saman, the udgitha, which is Om. Walk it slowly. The ground. The rain in it. What grows from the rain. The people fed by what grows. The voice those people have. The best words a voice can say. Then those words, sung. And the heart of the singing, one syllable. Each link is the rasa, the juice, the essence, of the one before it. So in this picture, a song isn't a pleasant extra laid on top of the words. It's what the words are reaching toward. The melody is the essence of the verse, the way the verse is the essence of speech. And Om sits at the end of a line that starts with dirt. That might be the part worth keeping. The Upanishad doesn't float the sacred syllable above ordinary things. It grows it from soil, water and food, through a body and a voice. Every Om, in this reading, has a field behind it.
screen: `THE UDGITHA: THE HIGH CHANT.` · `EARTH, WATER, PLANTS, PEOPLE, SPEECH.` · `VERSE, THEN MELODY, THEN OM.` · `EVERY OM HAS A FIELD BEHIND IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk the chain in your body. Sit, and feel the ground under you. Earth. Take a breath and think of the water in you. Water. Think of the last thing you ate, grown somewhere. Plants. Feel yourself here, sitting. A person. Then let a quiet sound come on the out-breath, a hum, a word, or Om if you use it. Speech, then song. Then rest in the quiet after the sound. Go around the chain again at your own pace. If you pray, you can rest in prayer at the end of it. The bell holds the time.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, the melody is the essence of the verse, and the high chant's heart is Om. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Sama Veda as song. Today, pick one thing on your table and follow its chain back three links. Notice where it started. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

fork.setup: you're following the Chandogya's chain. the essence of speech is the Rig Veda's verses. what is the essence of the verses?
fork.reveal: the melody. in this chain the verse sung is the essence of the verse, and the high chant's essence is Om.

original.note: Sanskrit: the high chant of a Sama Veda song. The Chandogya Upanishad opens by teaching it as Om.

trapdoor: what you thought: a melody is decoration on top of the words.
what it means: in the Chandogya, the melody is the essence of the verse, and Om is the essence of the chant.
what a scholar hears: rasa, juice or essence: each link (earth, water, plants, person, speech, ṛc, sāman, udgītha) is the rasa of the one before (Chandogya 1.1.2).
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 1.1.1 (meditate on Om as the udgitha, for one sings the udgitha beginning with Om)
Chandogya Upanishad 1.1.2 (the chain of essences from earth to the udgitha)

notes: Paraphrase of Chandogya 1.1.1–2: confirm the order of the chain (beings → earth → water → plants → person → speech → ṛc → sāman → udgītha) and the gloss of rasa as 'essence'.
Udgītha described as 'the part of a Sama Veda song the lead singer sends up' is a simplification of the udgātṛ's portion of the chant; confirm.
Max Müller's 1879 Upanishads translation is public domain but is not on the validator's list, so all English is paraphrase.
'Every Om, in this reading, has a field behind it' is an interpretive line; cut if a Keeper finds it too loose.
